is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.

citations.quote: A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

Let $P\subset S^2$ be the finite connected 4-valent graph underlying a regular link projection. Its complementary regions have exactly two colorings with two colors such that regions sharing an edge have different colors.

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.
For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.

derivations.claim: Measure the signed half-twist of a band relative to the planar framing of its two disk ends; call this incidence sign $\epsilon_e$. This is the unoriented crossing incidence, not the oriented link crossing sign. At two crossings joined by a projection edge, alternation changes which branch is over, while the chosen-color sector changes sides along that edge. The two changes cancel in the half-twist chart, giving the same incidence sign at the two crossings. Since the projection graph is connected, every band has one common sign $\epsilon$. Reversing the chosen orientation of a graph edge reverses its cycle coefficient, without changing this incidence sign.

We compute the normal pairing in the disk-and-band presentation. After clearing rational denominators, represent a cycle by finitely many oriented parallel strands through each band, joined by arcs in the vertex disks; any extraneous arc pairs can be canceled inside those disks. The signed number of strands through band $e$ is its graph coefficient $a_e$. Normal transfer gives two local pushoffs of each strand, exchanged at a one-sided passage. In an untwisted planar disk the contributions of the two normal sides to the mixed-crossing count cancel. In a band with a signed half-turn, each ordered pair of an original strand and a transferred strand contributes $\epsilon_e$ to the total pairing: one normal side passes from one side of the original strand to the other during the half-turn, and the other normal side makes the complementary passage; the two mixed crossings have the same incidence sign, and the linking count is half their signed sum. Reversing either strand orientation reverses the corresponding contribution. Consequently the contribution of that band is $\epsilon_e(\sum_i s_i)(\sum_j s_j)=\epsilon_e a_e^2$, where $s_i=\pm1$ are the strand orientations. This is also a direct computation with the half-twisted strip $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v\cos(\pi u),v\sin(\pi u))$, reversing the half-turn for the other sign. The strips' end collars are included in this count; crossings of joining arcs in the planar disks cancel between the two normal sides. Linking here can be computed by the signed mixed-crossing count because a finite oriented smoothing of the first curve gives spanning disks and crossing bands, whose intersections with the second curve give that count. This finite construction uses the supplied drawing and does not use a link-diagram invariance theorem. Summing over all bands and restoring rational coefficients gives $\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)=\sum_e\epsilon_e a_e^2$.

citations.quote: A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram on an oriented projection sphere. Choose either checkerboard color. Put a disk in each region of that color and join the opposite colored sectors at every crossing by a half-twisted band, with the twist chosen so that the boundary follows the over-under diagram. After rounding corners these disks and bands form a compact connected embedded spanning surface $F$ for the represented link. If $D$ has crossings, let $G$ be the corresponding Tait graph and orient its edges arbitrarily. Under the retraction of $F$ onto $G$, write a rational homology class as the unique graph cycle $a=\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e e$. There is a single sign $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ such that
$$q(a)=\epsilon\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e^2=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$$
for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ representing $a$, where $\tau c$ is its normal transfer. Thus $q$ is positive definite or negative definite on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. For a crossingless connected diagram, use either spanning disk and the zero-dimensional definite form.

Let $F\subset S^3$ be a compact connected smoothly embedded surface with nonempty boundary $L$, supplied with a finite disk-and-band presentation. The surface may be nonorientable. A normal transfer $\tau c$ of an oriented rational multicurve $c$ in the interior of $F$ is its total inverse image in the boundary of a sufficiently small normal interval neighborhood of $F$, oriented by projection onto $c$. Suppose a quadratic form $q$ on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ is positive definite or negative definite and satisfies $q([c])=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$ for every such rational multicurve. Then $L$ is nonsplit. Definiteness on the zero vector space is allowed.
